title: Hey, I'm building a game that uses battle scenes like the one below. As you can see consistency is an issue. I'm building an art pipeline an would love community input.
author: Natural-Captain-7333
selftext: Essentially I'm using Ai to make an asset engine for the game in the screenshot. Not strict to pixel art but that may be what it becomes. I've locked the plan of individual limb generation and smart skeletal structure as well as limb to limb generation for consistency. What else do you think would get this to a point where it's a production tool rather than a tested gimmick? No plans of monetizing it if it even works - purely just trying to make the art side of ai game dev easier.

comments.author: Sufficient_Art2594
comments.body:
I dont really have any input, I just want to say that I really like the overall UI and think its kinda neat and cozy. I think the character models look pretty decent as well. The background has that complex lighting pixelation that is a bit of a giveaway for AI generated stuff, but its not the worst.

I think the only things I would change are matching the foreground UI boxes and text to be MORE pixel style (or at least a stylistic change, it feels a bit cold for the rest of the aesthetic), and reduce some of the shadow/lighting pixel complexity for the background layer especially. The overall layering is pretty decent imo.

comments.author: ilicp
comments.body:
What am I looking at here? Multiple sprites or is this all done in one pass? 


I'll assume they're on separate sprites? Right? The background is awful - there's no advice besides nuke it and learn art fundamentals. Colour theory. Contrast and values. That background is just nonsense noise and an assault on my senses lol. 


How many images do you need? Are they animated? 
There are loads of cc0 images online that you can reference. If the sprites aren't animated and you don't need hundreds of them, just get references and trace them. A little bit of legwork on Asprite to have consistent designs and pallette that you can claim authorship of seems more worth it than an asset engine to make JRPG battle that's looking like a deep fried hallucination

replies.author: Natural-Captain-7333
replies.body: Mobile limited user - Ive heard of asprite but havnt looked into it much. I appreciate the honest feedback, if you care to give me dummy break down of asprite I am very untechnical

replies.author: ilicp
replies.body:
Sorry if I come off harsh too lol don't take me too seriously. Honestly I don't fully understand what you're making here either (asset engine and how it works?)


You can download Libresprite for free. It's just a software to draw and animate sprites. What I'm suggesting is the old school way without AI - literally trace over a reference picture or photo (you could even AI generate the image as a ref and then trace over it) -- if you don't need 1000s of animated sprites it might just be easier to draw them than to generate consistent AI results imho. 


I would still highly recommend learning some theory too... you're gonna bang your head on a wall trying to make art assets without understanding fundamental concepts in art. Nevermind the skill to draw and paint, that takes years of practice, but at least get started on understanding the theory so you can probably write better prompts and curate the output better.


When you trace over something you get to make changes. You get to choose the exact colors used (palette) - this gives you control - this gives consistency - it's also a fair amount of work though, I won't deny. 



Sorry this is turning into more like an anti-AI rant than helping with your asset engine. I just wonder if the asset engine is actually necessary for you - personally I think you'll benefit more by learning some art theory and just giving it a shot with Libresprite and tracing

replies.author: Natural-Captain-7333
replies.body: Haha no dude you’re good - very useful feedback. Not visually present in the post but I actually have been practicing on tracing ai gens onto a 128x128 canvas. Struggling with depth but I can see the difference drastically from the ai genned assets.

replies.author: ilicp
replies.body:
Nice.. I'm a newbie with sprites myself tbh. Watching a lot of AdamCYounis on youtube to learn more and see how someone else animates and draws tilesets etc. He will even talk about some art concepts and how to apply them in pixel art. Good channel.


For depth don't rush it and you also don't need to get everything looking game ready from the start. Use placeholders. As you improve you can go back and do more passes over older assets. You could maybe even feed your version back into AI to add depth but hopefully not make it too noisy again. Idk. I personally don't use AI for anything myself so I don't have a workflow that includes it. Whenever I try it honestly just feels more tedious that I end up deciding "screw it, I'll just learn to draw" lol. I'm not gonna say this is the best way to do it lol.. it's time consuming to learn and practice new skills but it does give you full control and I do actually enjoy the process of drawing/animating so it works out for me.


For my first animations I used the free "Unity-Chan" 3D model in unity, I recorded the run animation with orthographic camera, then I take that recording to Libresprite and I just rotoscope every frame. It is a bit tedious but it's easier than drawing it from scratch considering I'm not the best artist.


The sprites in Doom iirc were traced from clay models. They got an artist to make the clay models and then just took photos from each direction to make the sprite sheets :) old trick but it still works wonders to trace
